messages.author: 23e9c489ea8b313a
messages.subject: engine="julia" ?
parts:
As some of you may know, I have had a (rather late) mid-life crisis and run off with another language called Julia. (http://julialang.org)

It is a young language (release 0.2 is due out "real soon now").  Currently starting a julia process and loading various packages can be slow - on the order of a couple of seconds.  Writing a knitr language engine for Julia that started a new process for every chunk would probably be unacceptably slow at this point.  In addition it would be awkward to cache results for reuse in later chunks.

Has anyone experimented with a knitr language engine that execs a process and exchanges strings, say through a read-write pipe?

Right now I am using cut-and-paste from an ESS *julia* buffer in emacs into the .Rmd file but readers of this list know why that's not a good idea.

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] engine="julia" ?
parts:
That is *the* most challenging technical problem that I have been
struggling ever since the day one of knitr engines. If anyone knows
the answer to this general problem, joyful tears will be streaming
down my faces :)

A few months ago, my friend Yixuan told me FIFOs might be one way to
go: http://www.linuxjournal.com/content/using-named-pipes-fifos-bash

My knowledge in this area is quite limited. Ideally knitr should spawn
a process for each language engine, and keep listening on subsequent
code chunks.

How did ESS achieve that?

Regards,
Yihui
--

A few months ago, my friend Yixuan told me FIFOs might be one way to

My knowledge in this area is quite limited. Ideally knitr should spawn

code chunks.

How did ESS achieve that?

The ESS developers are much better qualified than I to answer that question.  I will give a hand-waving explanation but I would defer to those who know more than I do.

The basic design of ESS inferior processes is built on an interactive shell mode that did exactly this.  The code is carefully designed to be able to plug in new languages by creating a new configuration.  That is a vast simplification of a great deal of hard work, of course, but the answer is that it is reasonably straightforward because it was designed to be straightforward.

I asked this question at the Bioconductor 2013 conference today.
Although I did not get a 100% clear answer, I figured something out
later, but the problem now is Julia does not seem to accept code input
from pipes, e.g.

There is no output here. If you can figure out what is going on here,
I think I will add the Julia engine to knitr in five minutes.

Yes, we can use `julia -e` for every Julia code chunk, and that is
exactly where the problem comes from: for each chunk, a new Julia
session is opened.

And we cannot do something like `echo '1+1' | julia -e`, either.

Regards,
Yihui

parts:
Sorry to be late in responding - I'm travelling and have limited network access.
Running Julia to read from and write to a fifo is definitely possible but I am not sure of the details.  Keno Fischer demonstrated this at the Julia workshop at MIT in January.  He is more likely to be helpful to you on this than I am.
 
Keno:  Yihui is the author of the knitr package for R that transforms files in a noweb format mixing LaTeX and R sources or Markdown and R sources into LaTeX or Markdown by executing the R chunks.  There is provision for including chunks in other languages and I am particularly interested in creating a Julia REPL session that accepts input from a pipe and writes to a pipe.  That way a persistent Julia process could be used for evaluating the chunks.  If you are willing, it may be productive for you and Yihui to exchange some mail off-list.

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] engine="julia" ?
parts:
After slowly learning a tiny bit about Julia during the weekend, I
just succeeded with a prototype as illustrated here:
http://rpubs.com/yihui/julia-knitr

I first looked at the fifo (named pipe) approach, and it worked pretty
well, but it lacks portability, especially under Windows (I have no
idea how to create a fifo there). Then I experimented with socket
connections. It turns out to be usable, and I believe it is portable
to Windows as well.

I guess this might be a general solution to other languages, so I
packed what I have done into a small package:
https://github.com/yihui/runr

I still have a few questions, though:

1. The output is not really what we would have seen in Julia REPL,
e.g. [1:3] gives

3-element Int64 Array:
1
2
3

but I can only get [1,2,3] because I'm using println() to capture the
output: https://github.com/yihui/runr/blob/master/inst/lang/julia_socket.jl
I do not know how to faithfully reproduce the console output. A
related question is here: http://stackoverflow.com/q/17769065/559676
In particular, the side effects of print()/println() in the code will
be lost (no way to redirect stdout at the moment).

2. I have not used "try catch" yet; when the Julia code is
problematic, the process will be terminated.

3. I do not know how to find a usable TCP port in R. The default 2000
may not always be available.

4. I do not understand scopes yet, so the code might be evaluated in
the wrong environment. (what are globalenv() and parent.frame() in
Julia?)

There might be other problems. Please feel free to improve this
package. Eventually knitr will depend on it.

The Rmd source for that Rpubs post is:

# Run Julia from R

First we set up the Julia engine.

```{r setup}
library(knitr)
library(runr)
j = proc_julia()
j$start()
knit_engines$set(julia = function(options) {
knitr:::wrap(j$exec(options$code), options)
})
```

Test a sequence of numbers:

```{r test-a, engine='julia'}
a = [1:10]
a + 9
```

Test a function:

```{r test-b, engine='julia'}
b(x) = x^2 + 2x + 1
b(5)
x = {"a", "b", "c"}
```

Do not forget to shut it down in the end.

```{r quit}
j$stop()
```

Regards,
Yihui
--

Hi,
I know this is an old post, but I discovered it while looking for a way to call Julia from Pweave.

I discovered that it's very easy to call Python from  Julia and ended up writing Julia version of Pweave: https://github.com/mpastell/JuliaReport.jl, which uses Pweave for reading input and formatting output. The current version has optional terminal chunks and can capture PyPlot figures. See small sample: https://github.com/mpastell/JuliaReport.jl/raw/master/examples/julia_sample.pdf

Anyway I thought some people on this list might be interested in it. And please let me know if anyone is interested in collaboration possibly working on runr integration. Note that this is my first Julia project and I really don't know the language well.
